```{r}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(tidyverse)
options(scipen = 999)
```

### Introduction

In the class activity, you tested a school board member's claim using data from Montgomery County, Pa. — and found a model that didn't hold up. Now you'll run the same analysis using data from Montgomery County, Md. Your job is to evaluate whether the Maryland data tells a different story, and what that means for how you'd report on the claim.

### Loading the Data

```{r}
schools <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405_files/refs/heads/main/montgomery_md.csv")
```

### Task 1: Examine the Data First (2 points)

Before you plot anything, look at the data — you know why by now.

```{r}
summary(schools$`FARMS Pct`)
schools |> arrange(desc(`FARMS Pct`)) |> head(10)
```

Are there any data quality issues like the ones you found in the Pennsylvania data? How does the distribution of FARMS percentages compare between the two counties? Note anything that concerns you or gives you confidence in the data.

In the PA county, schools with a higher percentage of students receiving free and reduced-priced meals performed better on standardized test scores than the MD county with a higher percentage of students receiving FARMS. For example, Broad Acres Elementary in MD has a FARMS percentage of 96.0% and 39.4% of their students met or exceeded math expectations; Barth Elementary School in PA has a FARMS percentage of 100% and 60.3% of their students met or exceeded math expectations. This isn't necessarily a data quality issue, but it does show an inconsistency with the models that don't hold up the PA school board member's claim.

I would have more confidence in the data if I knew how many students were enrolled in these schools or who took the standardized math tests. 


### Task 2: Create a Scatterplot and Compare (5 points)

Replace the REPLACE_ME value with the correct variable name to create a scatterplot of FARMS percentage vs. math scores for Montgomery County, Md.

```{r}
schools |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `FARMS Pct`, y = `% Met or Exceeded Math Expectations`)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "FARMS Percentage", y = "% Met or Exceeded Math Expectations",
       title = "Math Scores vs. FARMS Percentage, Montgomery County MD")
```

Describe what you see. Then compare this scatterplot specifically to the Pennsylvania one: what differences do you notice in the direction, strength, and spread of the relationship? The two counties share a name and are both suburban — what might explain why they look so different?

I see a strong negative correlation between FARMS percentage and percentage of students who met or exceeded math expectations. The scatterplot shows that as the percentage of students who receive FARMS increases, students who meet or exceed math expectations decreases. 

In the PA schools scatterplot, the data was heavily skewed to the right because of some outliers, thus giving it a moderate positive relationship between the variables. Most of the data for the PA schools clustered with no correlation on to the low-end of the x-axis, but the extreme outliers pulled the regression line towards the right where FARMS percentage was at 100%.

Although the counties share a name and are suburban, the difference shown in the scatterplots could be attributed to different math curriculums, teaching styles, teacher pay and the school conditions (could a school in worse condition affect a student's productivity or material engagement?). How much the school district invests in the students differs, which could also explain why the data is distributed differently.


### Task 3: Linear Regression Model (5 points)

Replace the REPLACE_ME value with the correct variable name to run a linear regression model predicting math scores from FARMS percentage.

```{r}
model <- lm(`% Met or Exceeded Math Expectations` ~ `FARMS Pct`, data = schools)
summary(model)
```

Report the three key statistics: the p-value, the Adjusted R-squared, and the coefficient for FARMS Pct. Then interpret them together — not separately. What does the combination of these three numbers tell you about the relationship between poverty and math scores in Montgomery County, Md.? Is this model worth using? How does it compare to the Pennsylvania model?

The p-value is < 0.00000000000000022, adjusted R-squared is 0.6734 and the coefficient for FARMS percentage is 0.59511. The p-value suggests that the relationship is statistically significant, and we can reject the null hypothesis. The adjusted R-value (converted to 67.34%) suggests that 67.34% of the variance can be attributed to the independent variable, so that implies a moderately strong explanatory factor between the variables. The coefficient says that there is a moderate-to-strong relationship between the variables, and that the size of the relationship is moderate.  


### Task 4: Identifying Schools with the Biggest Residuals (6 points)

Replace the REPLACE_ME values with the correct variable names to calculate predicted values, residuals, and absolute residuals for each school. Then arrange the schools in descending order of absolute residuals.

```{r}
schools <- schools |>
  mutate(
    predicted = predict(model),
    residual = `% Met or Exceeded Math Expectations` - predicted,
    abs_residual = abs(residual)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(abs_residual))

head(schools |> select(1, `FARMS Pct`, `% Met or Exceeded Math Expectations`, predicted, residual), 10)
```

Identify the school with the largest positive residual (doing much better than the model predicts) and the school with the largest negative residual (doing much worse). For each school, find its zip code and look it up on [CensusReporter.org](https://censusreporter.org).

For each of the two schools, answer:
- What does the demographic and economic profile of the zip code look like?
- Does anything in that profile help explain why the school is over- or under-performing the model?
- What would your first reporting question be to the principal of that school?

The school with the largest positive residual is Fox Chapel Elementary (residual of 29.99/30), and the school with the largest negative residual is Germantown Elementary (-28.08). 

The demographic profile of Fox Chapel's zip code is majority residents between the ages of 18-64, majority Black residents (29%) and followed by Hispanic residents (25%). For the economic profile, children under 18 make up 21% of the poverty group, with 9.8% of persons below the poverty line. The median household income is $119,731 (±$10,256). The school may be over-performing because the majority of children under 18 do not experience poverty (79%), based on the data. This could boost student motivation and relieve them from financial stress. They may also have more financial access to school supplies or paid tutors. I would first ask the principal if the school offers accelerated learning programs that students could enroll in to improve their skills.

The demographic of Germantown Elementary's zip code is also majority people ages 18-64. However, their majority is close, with Black being 27% and White being 26%. Hispanic residents make up the third-most race and ethnicity profile with 22%. For the economic profile, the median household income is $115,022 ±$8,583. 11% of children under 18 experience poverty, and there are 8.3% persons below the poverty line. Germantown Elementary may be under-performing because of the race and ethnicity makeup-- there could be a language barrier between students and teachers that presents an obstacle to learning. I would ask the principal if there are is an ESL program, and if there is, how effective it is.



### Task 5: Evaluate the Model and Write the Pitch (7 points)

You've now run this analysis on two counties. Return to the school board member's claim: that elementary schools with fewer students on free and reduced-price meals do better on standardized math tests.

Write a short story pitch of 4-6 sentences that addresses all of the following: Does the Maryland data support or contradict the claim? How does it compare to what you found in Pennsylvania? What would you ask the school board member if you called them for comment? And what's the most interesting specific finding from your residuals analysis: which school would you want to visit first, and why?

The Maryland data contradicts the claim that the Pennsylvania school board member made, and an explanatory story is worth doing to examine how data does not support the idea that schools with a lower FARMS percentage do better than schools with a higher FARMS percentage on standardized math tests. When looking at the residuals, we see that Germantown Elementary (which has a lower FARMS percentage than Fox Chapel) under-performs in test scores. The Pennsylvania schools also have schools with large residuals/underperformance despite their relatively low FARMS percentage. I would ask the school board member about the PA schools with an 100% FARMS percentage-- what is the socioeconomic demographic for these schools, and why are the schools with a lower FARMS percentage falling behind in high math test scores? I would want to visit Fox Chapel Elementary in Maryland first to look at their math curriculum, their accelerated learning programs and other out-of-class programs aimed to helping students improve their skills.
